outcomes: A deployment edge admits exactly the declared routes and methods of a workload
An inventory in which a public route could reach a private one is refused before it is deployed
Go and TypeScript producers emit byte-identical inventories with the same digest for the same routes
Two pull requests that change different routes do not conflict on the committed inventory
A tool finds the pages that prove a feature requirement, and the path that renders each, with one read of the inventory
nonGoals: OpenAPI as an input: it cannot describe file-system routes, static outputs or public files, as ADR 0001 records
Framework-specific route discovery, which each framework owns
Cloud release ingestion, load-balancer reconciliation and provider resources

text: The protocol identifier is putnami.http-routes.v1 and the schema URL is https://putnami.dev/schemas/putnami-http-routes-v1.json.
The published schema carries that $id and pins that protocol, and its members match the Go types of the manifest, a route and its provenance.

An inventory parses strictly and fails as a whole: an unknown member or protocol, an unsupported pattern, an unsafe escape, a duplicate method or route, a missing provenance or publicEdge, and a malformed or mismatched digest are errors with stable codes.
Every valid fixture validates, every invalid one fails with its expected code, and every expected code is registered.
The TypeScript validator of @putnami/application gives every fixture the same verdict and code.
Two routes of one match language with a shared method are duplicates, whatever their parameter names.

Routes of different languages may overlap only when their visibility agrees: a public prefix, template or catch-all that could match a private route with a shared method is http_routes.visibility_overlap.
Overlap is computed on segment boundaries.

Canonicalization sorts methods and routes, serializes the protocol and the routes with two-space indentation and one trailing newline, and sets the digest to sha256: and the SHA-256 hex of those bytes.
The full fixture yields the committed cross-language golden and its pinned digest, whatever the route order and method case of the input, on every run.
The TypeScript serializer reproduces the golden bytes and digest without mutating its input.
The artifact form carries the digest; the committed form is the canonical artifact bytes without the digest member.
A strict parser accepts an inventory without a digest and returns it with the digest it computes, the one the artifact form carries; a present digest is checked as before.
The TypeScript validator of @putnami/application accepts the committed form of every valid fixture and derives the same digest.

The Go HTTP server describes its typed, manual, stream and static-mount routes, catch-all templates included, as an inventory that validates and is the same on every describe, and it fails on an anonymous wildcard.
The TypeScript extension merges the framework fragments into an inventory that validates and is the same on every run, and it fails on an unsupported pattern.
The page, action and static-asset routes of @putnami/web canonicalize and pass the strict parser.
A page route may carry proves, a list of {feature, requirement, at}: a feature ID, a requirement ID, and a concrete path the route admits.
Proves on another route, an empty or repeated list, a bad ID or an unadmitted at is http_routes.invalid_proof; a bad shape fails to parse.
The list sorts by feature, requirement and at; the digest covers it, and an inventory without it keeps its bytes.
The TypeScript validator of @putnami/application gives every proves fixture the same verdict and code.
